explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. God says, “You are not to make any gods alongside Me; you are not to make for yourselves gods of silver or gold.” (Exodus 20:23) He's just spoken from heaven, so He wants no made-up gods standing next to Him. I've stamped thousands of cookies, and not one of them ever ran my bakery.

explanations.answer: a king to rule over them
explanations.explanation: No king shows up in this verse. What God says they must not make is “gods of silver or gold.” (Exodus 20:23) A king would be a whole different conversation, and God isn't having it here.

explanations.answer: a tower that reaches the sky
explanations.explanation: Sky-high towers belong to another story, the builders in Genesis 11:4. Here God says nothing about a tower. He says they must not make “gods of silver or gold.” (Exodus 20:23) Same sky, different verse.

Not quite, friend. God doesn't pin His blessing to one mountain. He says, “In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you.” (Exodus 20:24) EVERY place. That's a lot bigger than Sinai.

That's right. Sinai isn't the limit. God says, “In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you.” (Exodus 20:24) Wherever He causes His name to be remembered, He promises to come and bless. That's a promise bigger than any one mountain.

Yes, defile it. God says, “for if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it.” (Exodus 20:25) So an altar of stones can't be built with stones shaped by tools. I love a sharp edge on a stamper, but God has His own rules for His altar, and I'm not touching those.

You'd think a chisel would make it sturdier, but that's not what God says. He says that if they use a chisel on the altar, they “will defile it.” (Exodus 20:25) He doesn't say anything about strength here. Just that the stones must not be shaped by tools.

A fancy chisel job feels like it would honor the altar, doesn't it? But God says the opposite: “if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it.” (Exodus 20:25) For this altar, tool-shaped stones are not the way. Keep the stones as they are.

explanations.answer: the Israelites were foreigners in Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, and it's right there in the verse. God says, “You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 22:21) They know what it's like to be the newcomer. Fine work, baker.

Nice try, but trade never comes up. The reason God gives is that “you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 22:21) The Israelites have been the newcomers before. That's the whole reason.
Taxes aren't in this verse at all. God points back to Egypt: “for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 22:21) He sends them back to their own story, not to anybody's wallet.

Yes. God says, “If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry.” (Exodus 22:23) Widows and orphans are not forgotten by Him. The word is “surely.” It's a heavy passage, but this part is a comfort.

The text says the opposite, friend. God says, “If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry.” (Exodus 22:23) He does hear them, with a “surely” on it. A mistreated widow or orphan has His attention.

Interest it is. God says the lender “must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest.” (Exodus 22:25) The man is poor, and he's one of God's people. So the loan comes without a charge on top.
Rent doesn't appear in this verse. What God says the lender must not charge is “interest.” (Exodus 22:25) The man borrowing is poor, so the loan stays a loan. Nothing gets added on.
Taxes aren't mentioned here. The word is “interest.” (Exodus 22:25) A poor man borrows money from a fellow Israelite, and God says not to charge him extra for it.

That's right. God says, “his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in?” (Exodus 22:27) It's his one blanket, so it goes home at sunset. If I had one apron and somebody kept it overnight, I'd be in a cold kitchen too.

explanations.answer: the neighbor needs it for worship
explanations.explanation: Worship isn't the reason God gives. He says, “his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in?” (Exodus 22:27) It's about the man staying covered at night. Plain and practical.

explanations.answer: keeping it overnight brings a curse
explanations.explanation: No curse is mentioned over the cloak. God's reason is that “his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in?” (Exodus 22:27) If the man cries out to Him, He says He will hear. The cloak is about the man's need.

Not this time, friend. God says, “do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit.” (Exodus 23:3) A few verses later He also says, “You shall not deny justice to the poor in their lawsuits.” (Exodus 23:6) So the court treats everyone fairly, and nobody gets a thumb on the scale.

That's right. God says, “do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit.” (Exodus 23:3) And He adds, “You shall not deny justice to the poor in their lawsuits.” (Exodus 23:6) Justice in the courtroom means fair for everybody.

Return it, yes. God says, “you must return it to him.” (Exodus 23:4) Even when it's your enemy's ox or donkey that's wandered off. Walking an enemy's animal home takes some serious self-control, friend.
Selling a stray animal would be tempting, but that's not the instruction. God says, “you must return it to him.” (Exodus 23:4) That's true even when the owner is your enemy. The ox goes home.
Renting out your enemy's stray donkey is a creative idea, I'll give you that. But the verse says, “you must return it to him.” (Exodus 23:4) The animal belongs to the enemy, so back it goes.

That's it. God says, “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous.” (Exodus 23:8) It even twists the words of the righteous. A bribe messes with everything it touches.
That's not what the verse says. God says a bribe “blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous.” (Exodus 23:8) The damage He names is to sight and to words.

Shame on a house isn't mentioned here. God says, “a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous.” (Exodus 23:8) That's the effect He names, and it's enough to stay far away from one.

explanations.answer: so the poor can eat from it
explanations.explanation: Right. God says the land rests “so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave.” (Exodus 23:11) The poor eat from the field, and the wild animals get the leftovers. Even the fields get a day off, and I'm a little jealous.

explanations.answer: so the priests can harvest it
explanations.explanation: Priests don't show up in this verse. God says the rest is “so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave.” (Exodus 23:11) The field is for the poor and the wild animals that year.

Road trips aren't mentioned. The reason God gives is “so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave.” (Exodus 23:11) That year the land is left to feed others.

Yes, the ox and donkey get a day off too. God says, “on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident.” (Exodus 23:12) Everybody in the household gets to rest. Even the donkey, who I'm sure has opinions.

The text says otherwise, friend. God says, “on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident.” (Exodus 23:12) The ox and donkey are right there in the list of those who rest.

That's the one. God says, “You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips.” (Exodus 23:13) He says it right after telling them to pay close attention to everything He's said. Don't even say their names.

Complaints aren't what this verse is about. God says, “You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips.” (Exodus 23:13) The names of other gods are the thing to keep off their lips.
Enemies' names aren't mentioned. What must not be heard on their lips is “the names of other gods.” (Exodus 23:13) That's the line God draws.
Right. God says they keep the feast in Abib “because that was the month you came out of Egypt.” (Exodus 23:15) The month itself is the reason. The unleavened bread points back to it.

explanations.answer: God gave the law that month
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that as the reason. God says they eat unleavened bread in Abib “because that was the month you came out of Egypt.” (Exodus 23:15) It's about leaving Egypt.

explanations.answer: the manna first fell that month
explanations.explanation: Manna isn't connected to Abib in this passage. The reason God gives is “because that was the month you came out of Egypt.” (Exodus 23:15) The feast points back to the day they left.
Not quite. God ends that verse with a clear rule: “No one may appear before Me empty-handed.” (Exodus 23:15) Everyone brings something when they come. Nobody shows up with nothing.
That's right. God says, “No one may appear before Me empty-handed.” (Exodus 23:15) The people come to the feast and they come with something in their hands. Showing up with nothing is out.

Yes. God says, “Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God.” (Exodus 23:19) The best. When I set out cookies for guests, I don't grab the crumbs from the bottom of the tray either.

Leftovers aren't what God asks for. He says, “Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God.” (Exodus 23:19) The best part of the firstfruits goes to the house of the LORD.

The smallest part isn't the instruction, friend. God says, “Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God.” (Exodus 23:19) It's the best part of the firstfruits. That's what He asks for.
